newsitem.title: INDIA: TEXT:India's credit policy for first half 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: TEXT:India's credit policy for first half 1997/98.

text.p: The following is the text of the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) monetary and credit policy for the first six months of 1997/98 (April-March) announced on Tuesday.
MONETARY AND CREDIT POLICY FOR THE FIRST HALF OF 1997-98
The growth rate of Broad money (M3) in 1996-97 was 15.6 per cent which was within the targetted band of 15.5 - 16.0 per cent. The real GDP is expected to have grown by 6.8 per cent.
The inflation rate as measured by the change in the Wholesale Price Index was 7.3 per cent on a point-to-point basis.
A notable feature of 1996-97 was that the money and foreign exchange markets were generally calm in contrast with the turbulence witnessed in these markets in the previous year.
A strong growth in bank deposits, coupled with substantial reduction in cash reserve requirements resulted in abundant liquidity in the system. However, the off-take of bank credit was subdued.

Short-term money market rates have moved down as a result of the easy liquidity conditions. Lending rates are known for their stickiness and remained at high levels during the first half of 1996-97 but softened later.

There has been a strong accretion to the foreign exchange reserves. The slow growth in non-food bank credit, the persistence of relatively high lending rates despite comfortable liquidity in the banking system and the acceleration of inflow of funds from abroad call for active monetary and exchange rate management by the Reserve Bank.

While the overall growth momentum has been sustained in 1996-97, divergent trends were observed in various sectors with agricultural output showing an impressive recovery and industrial growth slowing down.
Even within the industrial sector, the decline in growth rates in mining and electricity sectors was sharp. The inflation rate at 7.3 per cent was a matter of concern.
While manufacturing prices rose only by 5.1 per cent, primary articles recorded an increase of 8.3 per cent.

During 1996-97, procurement of foodgrains was low, while the off-take was high. With the result, buffer stocks of foodgrains fell from 23.3 million tonnes at the end of March 1996 to 18.6 million tonnes at the end of January 1997. The decline in wheat stocks was sharper.
MONETARY AND CREDIT DEVELOPMENTS

The target for expansion in M3 during 1996-97 was set at 15.5 - 16.0 per cent. During the financial year 1996-97, M3 increased by 940.49 billion rupees (15.6 per cent) as compared with an increase of 725.81 billion rupees (13.7 per cent) in 1995-96.
Reserve money increased by 55.14 billion rupees (2.8 per cent) during 1996-97 as compared with an increase of 251.75 billion rupees (14.9 per cent) during 1995-96.
The lower increase in reserve money reflected the sharp reduction in the cash reserve ratio and the decline in the utilisation of export credit refinance by banks.

Net Reserve Bank credit to Central Government showed an increase of 27.43 billion rupees (2.3 per cent) during the financial year 1996-97 as compared with a very large increase of 198.55 billion rupees (20.1 per cent) in 1995-96.
Commercial banks have increased their investments in government securities substantially in 1996-97 in the wake of low off-take of bank credit.

Net foreign exchange assets of the RBI witnessed a pronounced increase of 207.73 billion rupees (28.0 per cent) during 1996-97 as compared with a decline of 6.28 billion rupees (0.8 per cent) during 1995-96.
With a view to reducing volatility in call money rates, repos auctions were resumed in November 1996 and were further intensified during the last quarter of the financial year 1996-97.
The daily average repos outstanding during January - March 1997 amounted to 21.39 billion rupees.
The Reserve Bank also undertook active open market operations during 1996-97 to mop up excess liquidity from the financial system. The net sales amounted to 104.35 billion rupees during 1996-97.

Consistent with the working estimate of growth in aggregate deposits of scheduled commercial banks of 680.00 billion rupees (15.7 per cent) set for 1996-97, deposits showed a strong growth of 697.76 billion rupees (16.1 per cent) during 1996-97 as compared with a modest increase of 469.61 billion rupees (12.1 per cent) during 1995-96.
Time deposits registered a large increase of 613.00 billion rupees (17.4 per cent) in 1996-97 as compared with an increase of 432.49 billion rupees (14.0 per cent) in the previous year.
Food credit declined by 21.95 billion rupees during the financial year 1996-97 as compared with a decline of 24.83 billion during 1995-96.

Non-food credit of banks which had shown a continuous decline during the financial year upto August 16, 1996 except during one fortnight, increased thereafter continuously. The increase in non-food credit of scheduled commercial banks by 247.10 billion rupees (10.1 per cent) during 1996-97 was substantially lower than that of 449.38 billion rupees (22.5 per cent) during 1995-96.
The depressed capital markets seemed to have played a role inasmuch as there has to be some balance between debt and equity.

Equity raised by the corporates was significantly lower in 1996-97 than in 1995-96. Investments by banks in bonds/debentures/shares of public sector undertakings (PSUs) and private corporate sector and commercial paper increased by 65.77 billion rupees in 1996-97 as compared with a decline of 1.64 billion rupees in the previous year.

Thus, the total resource flow from banks to the commercial sector inclusive of loans and advances as well as investments in bonds/debentures/shares amounted to 312.87 billion rupees as against 447.74 billion in 1995-96.

Investments by scheduled commercial banks in Government securities showed a quantum jump with an increase of 268.60 billion rupees during 1996-97 as compared with the increase of 145.42 billion during 1995-96.
Viewed over a time horizon, say, three years (1994-95 to 1996-97), it would be seen that the average annual rate of growth of M3 is 17.2 per cent.
Average annual rate of growth of deposits of scheduled commercial banks is 17.0 per cent and the average annual rate of growth of non-food bank credit is 20.8 per cent.

One of the major objectives of financial sector reform has been to eliminate financial repression which is inherent in an administered interest rate structure and significant strides have been made in this direction.
This process of change which began in late 1980s has not been abrupt but gradual.
During this period, considerable degree of freedom has been given to banks to determine both deposit and lending rates.

Following moderation in the inflation rates in 1995-96 and 1996-97 and the reductions in cash reserve ratio, there has been a conspicuous reduction in both deposit rates and lending rates of banks as also spreads over the prime lending rates (PLR).

In July 1996, some public sector banks reduced their PLR by 0.5 percentage point. However, as a number of banks were charging lending rates far higher than PLR, banks were directed in the monetary policy announcement of October 1996 that along with the announcement of their PLR, they should, with the approval of their respective Boards, also announce the maximum spread over the PLR for all advances other than consumer credit.

The public sector banks have since reduced their PLR further from 16.5 per cent in March 1996 to 14.0 - 15.5 per cent by March 1997 and spreads in the range of 2.5 - 4.0 percentage points were announced.

During 1996-97, many banks had also brought down interest rates on term deposits by 1 to 2 percentage points on the shorter end of their maturity spectrum with a view to reducing the average cost of deposits.

Reflecting the easy liquidity conditions during 1996-97, there has been a significant softening of money market interest rates. At the short end of the market, the rates have come down conspicuously and have ruled generally low as compared with the levels prevailing in 1995-96.
The typical call money rates ruled low in the range of 2.00 - 5.00 per cent in the recent period.

The rate on 91 day Treasury bills came down from 12.97 per cent at the beginning of April 1996 to 7.96 per cent in March 1997. Similarly, the rate on 364 day Treasury bills declined from 13.12 per cent in April 1996 to 10.10 per cent in March 1997.
The typical rates of discount on Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and Commercial Paper (CP) have also declined sharply since end-March 1996.
There was also some softening of coupon rates on long-term Government bonds.
DEVELOPMENTS IN THE EXTERNAL SECTOR

The impressive rise in net capital inflows owing to the upsurge in non-resident deposits and portfolio investments coupled with a reduction in the current account deficit have augmented the Reserve Bank's foreign exchange reserves to $22.4 billion at end-March 1997, representing an increase of $5.4 billion over the year.
The balance of payments developments during 1996-97 continued to reflect signs of strength and sustainability of the external sector.
DEVELOPMENTS ON THE FISCAL FRONT
The Reserve Bank's support to the market borrowing programme during the fiscal year 1996-97 has been very limited in view of the very large investments in Government securities by commercial banks.
During 1996-97, the Central Government's lower dependence on net Reserve Bank credit has resulted in lower monetisation of deficit.

A bold and radical change which will strengthen fiscal discipline and provide greater autonomy to the Reserve Bank of India in conducting monetary policy in the coming years is the discontinuation with effect from April 1, 1997, of the system of ad hoc Treasury bills and 91 day Tap Treasury bills to finance the budget deficit and the introduction of a scheme of ways and means advances (WMA) by the Reserve Bank of India to the Central Government to accommodate temporary mismatches in the government's receipts and payments.
WMA will not be a permanent source of financing the government's deficit.
STANCE OF MONETARY POLICY FOR 1997-98

The stance of monetary policy in 1997-98 would be to achieve the twin objectives of maintaining reasonable price stability and ensuring availability of adequate bank credit to support the growth of the real sector.

The economy is still subject to inflationary pressures. There is need for continued caution on the price front and this would require a moderation in monetary expansion consistent with the expected real growth.
There is also the need for developing the Bank Rate as reference rate to signal policy stance of the Reserve Bank.
This would require rationalisation of the interest rate structure and linking of interest rates to the Bank Rate. There is an urgency to step up the flow of bank credit.
This would need streamlining and improving credit delivery system by giving greater freedom to banks.
Besides, banks must endeavour to bring down the interest rates by reducing the spreads. The money, foreign exchange and government securities markets need to be further developed and integrated.
In regulating money supply growth in the coming year, the Reserve Bank will have to reckon with the impact of capital inflows.

If capital inflows remain strong, the Reserve Bank must take care to see that the resultant reserve money expansion after taking into account the net RBI credit to the Central Government does not exceed a level that is consistent with the expansion in money supply justified by the growth of the real sector.

Wheat procurement during Rabi 1997 is expected to be 12 million tonnes and on the basis of this, food credit requirements are estimated to increase by Rs.3,600 crore during the first quarter (April - June 1997) and decline by Rs.2,300 crore in the second quarter (July - September 1997).
Banks must plan their credit operations accordingly.
The gross fiscal deficit of the Central Government for 1997-98 is placed at 4.5 per cent of GDP.
The extent of Reserve Bank's support to the Central Government is estimated at 160 billion rupees which, however, does not take into account open market operations.

The ultimate level of net RBI credit to Central Government will depend not only on the initial support to market borrowing programme but also on the passive and active open market operations of the Reserve Bank of India.

Given the real GDP growth of 6.0 - 7.0 per cent, monetary policy would seek to maintain the expansion in M3 in the range of 15.0 - 15.5 per cent to keep the inflation rate at around 6 per cent in 1997-98.
The projected increase in money supply may be reviewed and revised depending upon macro-economic developments.
On the basis of the projected increase in M3, the working estimate of the growth of aggregate deposits of scheduled commercial banks is placed at 800 billion rupees (16.0 per cent).

The expansion in net scheduled commercial bank credit including such investments as in bonds/debentures/ shares of PSUs and private corporate sector, is envisaged to be of the order of 20.0 - 21.0 per cent.
The policy measures which are being announced today have been so framed that banks will have adequate resources to meet all the genuine productive requirements of the economy.
CHANGES IN MEASURES
It is against this background, I am announcing the following measures:
(a) BANK RATE

The Bank Rate was raised to 11.0 per cent in July 1991 and further to 12.0 per cent in October 1991 against the backdrop of high inflation and difficult balance of payments situation. However, the rate remained at that level despite changes in the various economic parameters.
The Bank Rate as of now has only limited operational significance since the refinance rate is fixed at a lower level.

It is necessary to make the Bank Rate an effective signal rate as well as a reference rate. Accordingly, with effect from the close of business today (April 15, 1997), the Bank Rate will be reduced by one percentage point, i.e., from '12 per cent per annum' to '11 per cent per annum' so that changes in the Bank Rate reflect the stance of monetary policy.
All interest rates on advances from the Reserve Bank as also the penal rates on shortfalls in reserve requirements which are specifically linked to the Bank Rate will be revised.

These are indicated in Appendix I. Interest rates on other categories of accommodation from Reserve Bank, which are at present not linked to the Bank Rate, will now be linked to the Bank Rate as set out in Appendix II. A communication is being issued to banks seperately.
(b) RESERVE REQUIREMENTS
** Cash Reserve Ratio on Liabilities to Banking System **

At present, all scheduled commercial banks excluding regional rural banks (RRBs) are required to maintain a cash reserve ratio (CRR) of 10 per cent on liabilities to banking system computed as provided in Clause (d) of Explanation to Section 42(1) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

With a view to facilitating the development of a more realistic rupee yield curve and term money market, it has been decided to exempt liabilities to banking system from maintenance of cash reserve ratio of 10 per cent. Accordingly, with effect from the fortnight beginning April 26, 1997, liabilities to banking system of all scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs) as computed under Clause (d) of Explanation to Section 42(1) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 are exempted from maintenance of cash reserve ratio of 10 per cent.
As a result of reduction in CRR on liabilities to banking system an amount of Rs.950 crore of resources of banks would be released.
A notification of this change will be sent to banks separately.
** Statutory Liquidity Ratio on Liabilities to Banking System **

At present, all scheduled commercial banks (excluding regional rural banks) are required to maintain statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) on liabilities to banking system computed as provided in Clause (d) of Explanation to Section 18(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

It has been decided that with effect from the fortnight beginning April 26, 1997, all scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs) are exempted from maintenance of SLR on liabilities to banking system computed as provided in Clause (d) of Explanation to Section 18(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. A communication is being issued to banks separately.
** Cash Reserve Ratio on Non-Resident Deposits **

At present, liabilities under Foreign Currency Non-Resident Accounts (Banks) FCNR(B) Scheme, Non-Resident External (Rupee) (NRE) Accounts Scheme, Non-Resident Non-Repatriable Rupee (NRNR) Accounts Scheme are subject to prescription of zero cash reserve ratio (CRR).
With a view to bringing all liabilities to the public under the umbrella of reserve requirements, it has been decided to bring non-resident deposits under the purview of cash reserve ratio.

Accordingly, with effect from the fortnight beginning from April 26, 1997, all scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs) are required to maintain a CRR of 10 per cent on the increase in liabilities under FCNR(B) scheme, NRE Accounts scheme and NRNR Accounts scheme over the level outstanding as on April 11, 1997.
A notification on this change will be sent to banks separately.
(c) INTEREST RATES ON DEPOSITS
** Domestic Term Deposits **
At present, interest rates on domestic term deposits of scheduled commercial banks are subject to a prescription of 'not exceeding 10.0 per cent per annum' for maturity of 30 days and upto one year.

For maturity of over one year, banks are free to fix their own interest rates. It has been decided to reduce, effective from April 16, 1997, the maximum deposit rate for maturity of 30 days and upto one year and also link this rate to the Bank Rate.

Accordingly, with effect from April 16, 1997, the interest rate on domestic term deposits of maturity of 30 days and upto one year is changed from 'not exceeding 10.0 per cent per annum' to 'not exceeding Bank Rate minus two percentage points per annum'.
With the Bank Rate at 11 per cent, this will mean a rate 'not exceeding 9 per cent per annum'.
Banks should obtain the prior approval of their respective Boards for the deposit rates they will be offering on deposits of various maturities.

The revised term deposit rates will apply only to fresh deposits and on renewal of maturing deposits. The existing and the revised deposit rates are set out below: Scheduled Commercial Banks' Interest Rates on Term Deposits (excluding Non-Resident Deposits) (Per cent per annum) Existing New Duration.
** Interest Rates on Term Deposits under Non-Resident (External) Rupee (NRE) Accounts Scheme **

With a view to bringing about a better alignment of the interest rate structure of term deposits under Non-Resident (External) Rupee (NRE) Accounts Scheme with that on domestic term deposits, effective April 16, 1997, the interest rates on term deposits under NRE Accounts of over one year are being freed.

Furthermore, with a view to bringing the interest rates offered on term deposits under NRE Accounts on par with those on domestic term deposits, effective April 16, 1997, the interest rate offered on NRE term deposits of 6 months and upto one year is prescribed at 'not exceeding Bank Rate minus 2 percentage points'.

This would imply that the interest rate on term deposits of 6 months and upto one year would be 'not exceeding 9.0 per cent per annum'. Banks should obtain the prior approval of their respective Boards for the deposit rates they will be offering on deposits of various maturities.
The revised term deposit rates will apply only to fresh deposits and on renewal of maturing deposits.
Scheduled Commercial Banks' Interest Rates on Deposits under Non-Resident (External) Rupee (NRE) Accounts Scheme.
** Interest Rates on Deposits under Foreign Currency
Foreign Currency Non-Resident Accounts (Banks) FCNR(B) Scheme was introduced in April 1993.

Under this scheme, deposits are accepted at interest rates for specified maturities prescribed by RBI from time to time in four foreign currencies, viz., the Dollar, the Pound Sterling, the Deutsche Mark and the Japanese Yen and the foreign exchange risk is borne by the banks.
With a view to giving more flexibility to banks, it has been decided that banks may determine interest rates on such deposits subject to a ceiling prescribed by RBI from time to time.
A communication is being issued to banks separately.
(d) RATIONALISATION OF INTEREST RATES ON POST-SHIPMENT RUPEE EXPORT CREDIT

At present, interest rate on post-shipment rupee export credit upto 90 days is prescribed at 13.0 per cent per annum and for over 90 days and upto six months from the date of shipment it is 15.0 per cent per annum.

As part of a move to giving general operational freedom to banks and also taking into consideration the fact that some banks have shown willingness to extend post-shipment export credit at lower interest rates if export proceeds are realised in shorter periods, it has been decided that effective April 16, 1997, the interest rates on post-shipment rupee export credit upto 90 days be changed from the existing 13.0 per cent per annum to 'not exceeding 13.0 per cent per annum'.
Interest rate on export credit beyond 90 days and upto six months from the date of shipment would remain unchanged at 15.0 per cent per annum.
As before, in respect of post-shipment rupee export credit beyond 90 days, the higher rate of interest will apply only for the period beyond 90 days and not from the date of advance.
(e) RESERVE BANK REFINANCE
** Introduction of a General Refinance Facility **

In the context of a move from sector-specific refinance facilities to a general refinance facility and also with a view to enabling Bank Rate to emerge as a reference rate, a new refinance facility is being introduced, which would enable banks to tide over their temporary liquidity shortages.

Under the 'General Refinance Facility', effective from the fortnight beginning April 26, 1997, all scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs) will be provided General Refinance equivalent to 1.0 per cent of each bank's fortnightly average outstanding aggregate deposits in 1996-97, under Section 17(3B) of the Reserve Bank of India Act,1934.
Banks which avail of this facility beyond eight weeks would face an automatic debiting of their current accounts with the Reserve Bank.
Banks would, however, be able to avail of the General Refinance Facility afresh if there is a gap of two weeks during which there has been no borrowings under this facility.
The entitlement under this facility to the banking system will be of the order of 46.0 billion rupees.
Detailed operating instructions would be issued separately setting out limit for individual banks.
** Export Credit Refinance **

Export credit refinance limits of scheduled commercial banks, for the fortnight ended March 28, 1997, under the first tier (20 per cent of outstanding credit under the existing formula) were around 47.0 billion rupees of the total limits of 66.54 billion rupees.
The daily average utilisation during this fortnight was only 0.86 billion rupees forming 1.3 per cent of the limits.

As a move towards further rationalisation of export credit refinance to banks and in the context of introduction of a new General Refinance Facility, banks will be provided export credit refinance only on the basis of their incremental export credit.

With effect from the fortnight beginning April 26, 1997, scheduled commercial banks will be provided export credit refinance to the extent of 100 per cent of the increase in outstanding export credit eligible for refinance over the level of such credit as on February 16, 1996.
The rate of interest on export credit refinance will be at the Bank Rate (i.e., 11 per cent per annum).

With the introduction of the General Refinance Facility, there would be no reduction in the overall refinance entitlement of the banking system. Detailed operating instructions are being issued separately.
(f) MONEY MARKET

To further develop the money market and make it more efficient, a Standing Committee on Money Market similar to such Committees on Foreign Exchange Market and Government Securities Market is being set up to advise the Reserve Bank. Currently, the following measures are being taken :
** Routing of Transactions through DFHI **

In April 1991, policy relating to entry in the call/notice money market was liberalised and it was decided to provide access as lenders to such entities as were able to provide evidence to the Reserve Bank of India of bulk lendable resources subject, inter alia, to certain conditions one of them being that such transactions are to be routed through the DFHI only.
Hitherto, only two entities have been permitted by the Reserve Bank to operate in the call/notice money market as lenders through the DFHI.
It has been decided to extend the facility of routing call money transactions to entities through all the primary dealers with effect from the fortnight beginning April 26, 1997.
The minimum size of operation per transaction is also being reduced from 0.2 billion rupees to 0.1 billion.
A separate communication on the above measure is being issued to the primary dealers.
** Certificates of Deposit (CDs) **
The minimum size of issue of Certificates of Deposit to a single investor is being reduced from the existing 2.5 million rupees to 1.0 million rupees in multiples of 0.5 million rupees.
A communication on the above measure is being issued separately.
(g) DEVELOPMENT OF GOVERNMENT SECURITIES MARKET
** Ready Forward Transactions (Repos) and Reverse Repos **
In order to activate the Repos market so that it serves as an equilibrating force between the money market and the securities market, the following measures are being taken :
-- Instruments Eligible for Repo/Reverse Repo Transactions.

Repos are at present permitted among select institutions in Treasury bills of all maturities and Government of India dated securities which are approved by the Reserve Bank of India in consultation with the Government of India.

It has been decided to extend such repo/reverse repo transactions among such institutions in respect of all dated Central Government securities besides Treasury bills of all maturities. A separate communication will follow.
-- Participants in Reverse Repo Market.

It has been decided to allow non-bank entities who are holders of SGL Account with the Reserve Bank of India to enter into reverse Repo transactions with banks/primary dealers in Treasury bills of all maturities and all dated Central Government securities.

The first leg of the transaction by non-bank entities should be by way of purchase of securities eligible for Repos from banks/primary dealers and the second leg will be by way of selling back securities to banks/primary dealers.

Non-bank entities are, however, not allowed to enter into Repo transactions with banks/primary dealers. The transactions have to be effected at Mumbai. Detailed communication on this measure is being issued to banks separately.
** Treasury Bills of Varying Maturities **

In an effort to build an active Treasury bill market, 91 day Treasury bill auctions were introduced in January 1993, following the regular auctions for 364 day Treasury bills introduced earlier in April 1992.
There is an urgent need for further activating Treasury bill market, particularly in the context of the discontinuance of 91 day Tap Treasury bills and the system of ad hoc Treasury bills.
It is, therefore, proposed to issue Treasury bills of various maturities to facilitate the cash management requirements of various segments of the economy.
These auctions will be separately announced by the Reserve Bank.
(h) IMPROVING CREDIT DELIVERY SYSTEM
** Credit to Agriculture **
During 1996-97, the share capital of National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) was increased by Rs.500 crore to 10.0 billion rupees.
During the current year, a further increase of 5.0 billion rupees is proposed, raising the capital to 15.0 billion rupees and taking Reserve Bank's contribution to 10.5 billion rupees.
This is expected to enable NABARD to effectively leverage its equity and mobilise additional resources for investment credit.
The limit under the General Line of Credit (GLC) provided by the Reserve Bank of India to NABARD for short-term Seasonal Agricultural Operations, etc., stood at 55.0 billion rupees in 1996-97.
In order to accelerate the flow of production credit to agriculture, the financial accommodation is being further increased by 2.0 billion rupees taking the aggregate limit to 57.0 billion rupees.
** Credit to Small Scale Industry **

-- Banks are at present required to assess working capital needs of borrowers on the basis of 20 per cent of the projected turnover of village, tiny and other SSI units having working capital limits upto 0.1 billion rupees.
This simplified procedure is now being extended to borrowers having working capital limits upto 0.2 billion rupees from the banking system.

-- The limit on investment in the small scale industries sector is being enhanced by the Government from the present level of 6.0 million rupees (7.5 million rupees in the case of export oriented and ancillary units) to 0.3 billion rupees and for the tiny sector from 0.5 million rupees to 2.5 million rupees.

In this context, it has been decided that out of the funds available to all segments of the SSI sector, banks should ensure that 40 per cent will be made available for units with investment in plant and machinery upto 0.5 million rupees, 20 per cent for units with investment between 0.5 milllion rupees and 2.5 million rupees and the remaining 40 per cent for other SSI units. Operating instructions are being issued separately.
** Consortium Lending **
As banks are aware, the threshold limit for obligatory formation of consortium in respect of working capital finance was raised from 0.5 billion rupees to 5.0 billion rupees in October 1993.

The banks were also then given option to organise, at their discretion, syndication for extending credit for highly rated borrowers enjoying working capital facilities of 5.0 billion rupees and above.

As a measure of introducing flexibility in the credit delivery system and to facilitate smooth flow of credit, ground rules in respect of consortium arrangement - whether formed on voluntary or obligatory basis - were left to the judgement of the participating banks in October 1996.

In order to introduce further flexibility in the credit delivery system, it has been decided that it would not be obligatory on the part of banks to form a consortium even if the credit limit per borrower exceeds 5.0 billion rupees.
The need based finance required by the borrowers may, therefore, be extended by banks either entirely on their own, subject to observance of exposure limits or in association with other banks.

As an alternative to sole/multiple banking/consortium arrangement, banks are free to adopt syndication route, irrespective of the quantum of credit involved, if the arrangement suits the borrower and the financing banks.
** Loan System for Delivery of Bank Credit **

A 'Loan System' introduced in April 1995, with a view to imparting an element of discipline in the utilisation of bank credit, has been extended in phases to cover larger number of borrowers with the percentage of the 'loan component' of the working capital limit being gradually enhanced.
It has now been decided to effect the following further modifications in the system.

-- In the case of borrowers enjoying working capital credit limit of 2.0 billion rupees and above from the banking system, the loan component is being raised to 80 per cent as against 75 per cent at present.
-- In the case of borrowers enjoying working capital credit limit of 1.0 billion rupees and above but less than 2.0 billion rupees, loan component is be
ing raised to 75 per cent as against 60 per cent at present.

-- As regards borrowers with a limit of less than 1.0 billion rupees, it is not the intention to prescribe the level of loan and cash credit components, which, ideally may be settled between the bank and the customer; this category of borrowers may like to avail of the limit as loan since it will bestow to them the benefit of interest at the rate applicable on the loan component.
-- In respect of certain business activities which are cyclical and seasonal in nature or have inherent volatility, the strict application of loan system may create difficulties for the borrowers.
Banks, may with the approval of their respective Boards, identify such business activities which may be exempt from the loan system of delivery.
Keeping in view the convenience to borrowers, the following changes are being made in the 'Loan System':

(a) The minimum period of loan could be fixed by the concerned banks. Consistent with the enhancement in loan component, its spread over various maturities may be decided by banks, subject to roll-over.

(b) The financing bank, may permit borrowers to invest their short term/temporary surplus in short term money market instruments like Commercial Paper (CP), Certificates of Deposit (CDs) and in Term Deposit with bank, etc.
Detailed operating instructions will be issued separately.
** Assessment of Working Capital Requirements **
Consistent with the policy of liberalisation, it has now been decided to allow full operational freedom to banks in assessing the working capital requirements of borrowers.
Accordingly, banks are now free to evolve their own methods of assessing the working capital requirements of borrowers within the prudential guidelines and exposure norms, already prescribed.
The turnover method, as already prevalent for small borrowers, may continue to be used as a tool of assessment for this segment.
Since major corporates have adopted cash budgeting as a tool of funds management, banks may follow cash budget system for assessing the working capital finance in respect of large borrowers.
Individual banks may also, if they so decide, retain the present Maximum Permissible Bank Finance system, with necessary modifications or any other system.
The loan policy in respect of each broad category of industry shall be laid down by every bank with the approval of its Board.

All instructions relating to Maximum Permissible Bank Finance are being withdrawn. However, the Reserve Bank instructions relating to directed credit (such as priority sector, export, etc.), quantitative limits on lending (such as against shares and for consumer durables, etc.) and prohibition of credit (such as bridge finance, rediscounting of bills earlier discounted by NBFCs, etc.) shall continue to apply.
Detailed operational instructions in this regard are being issued separately.
(i) INVESTMENTS IN SHARES OF CORPORATE BODIES
At present, banks are allowed to invest in the debentures/ bonds/ shares of private corporate bodies and PSU shares upto 5 per cent of their incremental deposits in the previous year.
Within this ceiling banks are also allowed to purchase such debentures/bonds/shares in the secondary market (other than inter-bank transactions).

It has now been decided to exclude from this limit investments in preference shares/debentures/ bonds of private corporate bodies. In other words, the limit will be applicable for investments in ordinary shares of corporates, including PSUs.
Detailed communication on this change is being issued to banks separately.
(j) ADVANCES AGAINST SHARES

In view of the current state of capital markets, it has been decided to allow banks to extend loans to corporates against shares held by them to enable such corporates to meet the promoters' contribution to the equity of new companies in anticipation of raising resources.

Such loans will be treated as banks' investment directly in shares and would thus come under the ceiling of 5 per cent. The margin and the period of repayment of such loans will be determined by banks.
Detailed communication on this change is being issued to banks separately.
(k) BANK LENDING TO NON-BANKING FINANCIAL COMPANIES(NBFCs)
Lending by banks to NBFCs is presently restricted upto certain multiples of the latters' net owned funds (NOF). Similar ceilings have been prescribed for lending to NBFCs by financial institutions.

As part of the efforts to give greater operational freedom to banks, it has been decided to remove the existing overall limits of bank credit to such of the NBFCs as have fully complied with the requirements of registration, credit rating and prudential norms.
Accordingly, banks may determine the level of credit to such NBFCs.
Detailed operating instructions are being issued separately.
(l) COMMERCIAL PAPER

Commercial Paper (CP) can be issued at present by corporate customers and primary dealers in Government securities subject to the terms and conditions laid down in the 'Non-Banking Companies (Acceptance of Deposits through Commercial Paper) Directions, 1989' and 'Primary Dealers (Acceptance of Deposits through Commercial Paper) Directions, 1996', respectively.
These Directions require that commercial paper shall be issued for maturities between three months and less than one year from the date of issue.
It has now been decided to bring down the minimum period of maturity of CP to 30 days.
Detailed instructions in this regard are being issued separately.
(m) TRADE RELATED ADVANCES TO EXPORTERS OUT OF EXCHANGE EARNERS FOREIGN CURRENCY ACCOUNTS (EEFC)

To enable exporters to make trade-related advances without prior approval of Reserve Bank of India, it has been decided to permit corporate exporters to extend trade-related advances to their importer-clients provided such an advance is made out of EEFC accounts and provided that the total outstanding of such advances in respect of an EEFC account does not exceed $ 3.0 million.
A separate communication is being sent to authorised dealers.
(n) LENDING AND BORROWING OF FUNDS BY BANKS IN INDIA THROUGH THEIR OFFICES/CORRESPONDENTS ABROAD

In order to achieve greater integration between domestic and overseas money markets, authorised dealers will be permitted to borrow upto $10 million from their overseas offices/correspondents without any conditions on end use and repayment of such borrowings.
Simultaneously, authorised dealers will be permitted to invest funds in overseas money market instruments upto US $ 10 million.
Separate circular is being issued setting out the guidelines in this regard.
(o) PROPOSALS FOR DEEPENING AND WIDENING THE FOREX MARKET
** Forward Cover Based on Business Projections **
At present, before a forward contract is booked, authorised dealers have to satisfy themselves through documentary evidence that there is an underlying exposure.
In case of exporters and importers, the underlying document is usually a letter of credit or a firm order.
In case of borrowers, the loan document is taken as evidence.
As the period for receipt/payment for exports and imports is usually six months, forward contracts beyond six months are not normally booked.
Exporters/Importers may, however, like to take forward contracts based on their likely receivables and payables and business projections.
It is proposed to allow exporters and importers to take forward cover without the requirement of documentary evidence of a firm order or letter of credit.

Authorised dealers can, instead, without any limitation on the period of such contracts, book such contracts on the basis of a declaration of exposure supported by past performance and business projection.
It should, however, be ensured that the total forward contracts outstanding at any point of time does not exceed the average export/import turnover of the last two years.
This measure is expected to impart flexibility to corporates and improve liquidity in the forward markets for periods beyond six months also.
** Development of Rupee-Forex Swap Market **
Several corporates who have foreign exchange exposures arising out of external borrowing are now unable to obtain long-term forward cover for such exposures.
They, therefore, go in for the six month roll-over forward cover. There are corporates in the system who may be willing to convert some or whole of their rupee liabilities into forex liability.

RBI has been approving rupee foreign currency swaps between such corporates on a case by case basis. It is now proposed to allow authorised dealers to run a swap-book within their open positions/gap limits to enable them to arrange such swaps without RBI's prior approval.
Such a measure will enable those requiring long-term forward cover (including banks) to hedge themselves without altering the external liability of the country.
Detailed guidelines on the above measures will be issued separately.
SUMMING UP
The policy announced today aims at maintaining monetary expansion within the range of 15.0 - 15.5 per cent with a view to moderating the price increase.
The process of smoothening the credit delivery system and rationalisation of interest rate structure are expected to bring down the interest rates.
The provision of additional share capital and increase in limit under GLC to NABARD will accelerate the flow of credit to agriculture.
The measures announced relating to SSI units should benefit a greater number of units and enhance the availability of credit to SSI sector.
In response to the initiatives announced, the money market, the government securities market and the foreign exchange market will acquire greater depth.
A closer integration of these markets would enable effective transmission of monetary policy impulses.
Bank Rate should emerge as an effective reference rate.
